title: Aksum: Africa's Lost Empire

cards.h: An empire that minted gold in Africa
cards.b:
Aksum was a kingdom in what is now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea. From about the 1st to the 8th century CE it was one of the four great powers of the late ancient world, along with Rome, Persia and China.

Aksum is often left out of world history. Its story shows how Africa was connected to the Mediterranean, Arabia and India long before the age of European exploration.

cards.h: A port on the Red Sea
cards.b:
Aksum's wealth came from trade through its port of Adulis on the Red Sea. Ships carried ivory, gold and rhino horn out of Africa, and brought back textiles, glass, wine and olive oil from the Roman world.

A 1st-century Greek sailing guide, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes the trade of Adulis. It shows that the port was busy with merchants from many lands.

King Ezana converted to Christianity in the 4th century, around the 330s CE. The monk Frumentius, from the Phoenician city of Tyre, who had been shipwrecked as a boy, served at the court and was later sent to Alexandria, where he was ordained as the first bishop of Aksum.

Ezana's inscriptions, written in Ge'ez, Greek and Sabaean, mark his change of faith. Aksum became one of the earliest Christian kingdoms outside the Roman world.

King Ezana's inscriptions (4th century CE)

Ezana had stone inscriptions made in three languages. They describe his campaigns against peoples to the south and west, and they show a change from the older gods of Aksum to Christian faith.

They are among the richest texts for early African history, and they are a key source for scholars of Aksum.
Aksum rose on trade and faded as trade routes changed. Its decline came slowly, over centuries, and its capital moved inland.

Aksum minted its own coins in gold, silver and bronze. These were among the first coins in sub-Saharan Africa. They show a state with a sophisticated monetary system, and they carried the names and images of its kings.

The coins were used in trade with the Roman world, Arabia and India. Their design changed over time, showing the state's shifting faith and power.

Aksum raised huge carved stone pillars, called stelae, some as tall as thirty metres. They mark royal tombs and were carved to look like multi-storey buildings. The largest fell and broke, and it was later returned from Italy to Ethiopia in 2005.

The stelae show the skill of Aksumite stonemasons and the pride of its rulers. They are now among Ethiopia's most treasured monuments.

cards.h: Is the Ark of the Covenant in Aksum?
cards.b:
Ethiopian tradition claims that the Ark of the Covenant is kept in a chapel in Aksum. It is a powerful story that links the city to the Bible.

Scholars treat the claim as a religious tradition, not an historical fact. No outside researcher has been allowed to see the object, and it cannot be verified. The belief is important to Ethiopian Christians, but historians do not treat it as evidence.

Aksum's trade was hit by the rise of new powers in Arabia and Iran, and the spread of Islam in the 600s and 700s changed Red Sea trade. The interior became more important, and the state moved its centre inland.

Historians argue about the causes. Some stress climate change and drought, others point to changing trade routes and the rise of new cities. The decline was a slow shift rather than a sudden collapse.

Aksum was one of the earliest Christian states in the world. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church traces its roots to the Aksumite kings and the early bishops. This long Christian tradition still shapes Ethiopian identity.

Ethiopia was never fully colonised by a European power, except for a brief Italian occupation in the 1930s. Historians often point to Aksum's long history as part of that independence.

In the 4th century the Gupta empire was minting gold coins in India, as Aksum was minting its own gold. The two kingdoms were on opposite ends of the Indian Ocean trade system.

Indian cloth and spices moved through the Red Sea ports, and Aksum's traders were part of the same network. Coins from both kingdoms show how trade could link distant states.

Five things to remember
  1. Aksum was based in the northern Ethiopian highlands.
  2. Its port was Adulis on the Red Sea.
  3. King Ezana converted to Christianity around the 330s.
  4. Aksum minted its own gold, silver and bronze coins.
  5. Its decline came slowly, from the 600s onward.
Think about it
  • Why is Aksum often left out of world history?
  • How did religion and trade shape each other in Aksum?
